concepts.title: Fourier series: why the method works
concepts.explain: Project one period of a function onto orthogonal sines and cosines. Each coefficient measures the amount of one frequency. Endpoint conditions tell us whether to use sine, cosine, or half-integer frequencies.
concepts.conditions: The period is $2l$. For a piecewise smooth function, the series converges to the function at continuity points and to the average of the one-sided limits at jumps.
concepts.proof:
To extract one coefficient, use orthogonality on $[-l,l]$: $\int_{-l}^l\cos(n\pi x/l)\cos(m\pi x/l)dx=0$ for $n\ne m$, while the same-frequency squared integral is $l$. Product-to-sum identities verify these integrals.

Multiply the expansion by $\cos(m\pi x/l)$ and integrate. Sines, the constant, and other frequencies vanish, leaving $a_ml$. Thus $a_m=\frac1l\int_{-l}^l f(x)\cos(m\pi x/l)dx$, $m\ge1$.

To extract a sine coefficient, multiply by $\sin(m\pi x/l)$ instead, giving $b_m=\frac1l\int_{-l}^l f(x)\sin(m\pi x/l)dx$. Integrating the expansion itself gives $a_0=\frac1l\int_{-l}^l f(x)dx$; the constant is $a_0/2$.

This derives projection coefficients, not the convergence theorem. Apply orthogonality to finite sums and then pass to an appropriate square-integrable limit. Pointwise sums require the Fourier convergence theorem for piecewise smooth functions; jumps give the average of the side limits.

example.question: Expand $f(x)=x$ on $(-\pi,\pi)$.
example.solution:
Here $l=\pi$. Since $f(x)=x$ is odd, multiplying by cosine stays odd, so $a_0=a_n=0$. Only sine coefficients remain.

Use $b_n=\frac2\pi\int_0^\pi x\sin(nx)dx$. With $u=x$ and $v=-\cos(nx)/n$, the integral is $\int_0^\pi x\sin(nx)dx=-\pi(-1)^n/n$.

Thus $b_n=2(-1)^{n+1}/n$, giving $x=2\sum_{n\ge1}(-1)^{n+1}\sin(nx)/n$ for $-\pi<x<\pi$. At the periodic seam, side limits $\pi$ and $-\pi$ average to zero.

concepts.memory: Check the period, then parity. Calculate projection integrals last.

concepts.title: Fourier transforms: why the method works
concepts.explain: The Fourier transform splits a whole-line function into a continuous range of frequencies. Differentiation becomes multiplication by $ik$ in frequency space. A narrow pulse has a broad spectrum. Throughout this chapter, the forward transform has no prefactor and the inverse has $1/(2\pi)$.
concepts.conditions: Usually require integrability or square integrability. Step functions, the sign function, and Coulomb potentials require distributions or regularization.
concepts.proof:
We derive two useful properties here, rather than prove the full Fourier inversion theorem. Assume sufficient integrability of the function and derivative, and vanishing boundary terms at infinity.

Integrate $\mathcal F[f^{\prime}](k)=\int f^{\prime}(x)e^{-ikx}dx$ by parts: $\int f^{\prime}e^{-ikx}dx=[fe^{-ikx}]_{-\infty}^{\infty}+ik\int fe^{-ikx}dx$. The derivative and integration-by-parts minus signs cancel.

With zero boundary term, $\mathcal F[f^{\prime}]=ikF$. Differentiating twice gives $(ik)^2F=-k^2F$, explaining why spatial differential equations simplify in frequency space.

For scaling, set $y=ax$, $a\ne0$. If $a<0$, reversed integration limits cancel the sign in the differential. Hence $\mathcal F[f(ax)](k)=|a|^{-1}F(k/a)$; retain the absolute value.

example.question: Find the transform of $f(x)=e^{-a|x|}$ for $a>0$.
example.solution:
The function $e^{-a|x|}$ is real and even. Cancel the sine imaginary part to get $F(k)=2\int_0^\infty e^{-ax}\cos(kx)dx$.

First integrate $\int_0^\infty e^{-(a-ik)x}dx=1/(a-ik)$, then take the real part. The upper-end exponential vanishes because $a>0$.

Rationalize as $1/(a-ik)=(a+ik)/(a^2+k^2)$, yielding $F(k)=2a/(a^2+k^2)$. Check that $F(0)=2/a$ equals the original area.

concepts.memory: Use a negative exponential for the forward transform and a positive one for the inverse. Keep track of $2\pi$ in product and convolution formulas.

concepts.title: Shifts, derivatives, and convolution in Fourier transforms
concepts.explain: The transform turns spatial derivatives into algebraic multiplication and convolutions into products. Before using a property, check the exponential sign and which side contains $2\pi$.
concepts.conditions: The convention is $F(k)=\int f(x)e^{-ikx}dx$ and $f(x)=(2\pi)^{-1}\int F(k)e^{ikx}dk$. For ordinary functions, require sufficient integrability, justified interchange of integrals, and vanishing integration-by-parts boundary terms. Distributional versions follow by definition.
concepts.proof:
Differentiation: integrate $\int f^{\prime}(x)e^{-ikx}dx$ by parts. Under the required decay conditions, the boundary term vanishes and leaves $ikF(k)$.

Translation: set $y=x-a$, so $x=y+a$ and $e^{-ikx}=e^{-ika}e^{-iky}$. Pull out the factor independent of $y$ to obtain $e^{-ika}F(k)$.

Convolution: write $(f*g)(x)=\int f(s)g(x-s)ds$. In the double integral put $y=x-s$, splitting the exponential as $e^{-iks}e^{-iky}$. The two integrals separate into $F(k)G(k)$.

Product: substitute $f(x)=\frac1{2\pi}\int F(q)e^{iqx}dq$ into the transform. After interchanging integrals, the inner one is $G(k-q)$, leaving $\frac1{2\pi}\int F(q)G(k-q)dq$. Its prefactor comes from inversion.

example.question: Given $\widehat{e^{-x^2}}=\sqrt\pi e^{-k^2/4}$, find the transform of $e^{-(x-a)^2}$.
example.solution:
Write $g(x)=e^{-(x-a)^2}$ as $f(x-a)$ with $f(x)=e^{-x^2}$. This identifies a translation without new integration.

Use the known $F(k)=\sqrt\pi e^{-k^2/4}$ and multiply by the translation factor: $G(k)=e^{-ika}\sqrt\pi e^{-k^2/4}$.

For real translation $a$, $|e^{-ika}|=1$, so only phase changes. An extra real growth factor suggests that $i$ was omitted from the exponent.

concepts.memory: A spatial shift adds phase. A derivative multiplies by ik. A convolution becomes a product.

concepts.title: The δ distribution and sampling
concepts.explain: Think of $\delta$ as a sampling rule acting on test functions. It is not an ordinary function that can be manipulated pointwise as “infinite at one point.” Pulses with unit area and shrinking width can approach it.
concepts.conditions: The second formula requires simple roots. The integration interval must contain the relevant roots.
concepts.proof:
A simple root matters because $g(x_j)=0$ and $g^{\prime}(x_j)\ne0$ allow a local inverse $x=x(u)$ with $u=g(x)$ and a finite inverse derivative.

Changing variables inside a test-function integral introduces $1/|g^{\prime}(x(u))|$. The absolute value accounts for orientation reversal near a root; do not divide by a signed derivative.

$\delta(u)$ samples at $u=0$, so this root contributes $\varphi(x_j)/|g^{\prime}(x_j)|$. Sum the contributions of all simple roots within the integration interval.

For a multiple root with $g^{\prime}(x_j)=0$, the substitution fails; the formula cannot be used by dividing by zero. Roots outside the interval contribute nothing, while endpoint roots require a stated convention.

example.question: Evaluate $\int_{-2}^2 (1+x^2)\delta(x^2-1)dx$.
example.solution:
Solve $x^2-1=0$ to get $x=\pm1$, both inside $[-2,2]$.

Calculate $g^{\prime}(x)=2x$. Its absolute value is two at both roots, so $\delta(x^2-1)=[\delta(x-1)+\delta(x+1)]/2$.

Finally evaluate the weight $1+x^2$ at each root, obtaining two each time. The integral is $2/2+2/2=2$; keeping only the positive root loses half the result.

concepts.memory: Find the roots → divide by the absolute derivative → sample the remaining function.

concepts.title: Laplace transforms: why the method works
concepts.explain: The Laplace transform uses only $t\ge0$. Its decaying exponential allows a larger class of functions to be transformed and is especially useful for initial-value problems. Transforming a derivative automatically includes the initial values.
concepts.conditions: $f$ is piecewise continuous and of exponential order. $\operatorname{Re}p$ must exceed its growth rate.
concepts.proof:
Begin with the definition. Assume suitable piecewise smoothness and exponential growth bounds for $f$ and the required derivatives, and take $\operatorname{Re}p$ large enough to eliminate the boundary term at infinity.

Integration by parts in $\int_0^\infty f^{\prime}(t)e^{-pt}dt$ gives $[fe^{-pt}]_0^\infty+p\int_0^\infty fe^{-pt}dt$. The upper value is zero and the lower value $f(0^+)$ is subtracted, leaving $pF-f(0^+)$.

Apply the same formula to $f^{\prime}$: $\mathcal L[f^{\prime\prime}]=p\mathcal L[f^{\prime}]-f^{\prime}(0^+)=p^2F-pf(0^+)-f^{\prime}(0^+)$. Initial displacement and velocity have different factors.

Initial-value terms are the boundary terms left by the lower integration limit. Write them explicitly before collecting the algebraic equation in an initial-value problem.

example.question: Find $\mathcal L[t e^{2t}]$.
example.solution:
Start from $\mathcal L[e^{2t}]=1/(p-2)$, convergent for $\operatorname{Re}p>2$.

Multiplication by $t$ gives the negative transform derivative: $\mathcal L[te^{2t}]=-\frac d{dp}(p-2)^{-1}=(p-2)^{-2}$. The derivative minus sign cancels the property’s minus sign.

Alternatively integrate $\int_0^\infty t e^{-(p-2)t}dt$ by parts to get the same result. The polynomial factor $t$ does not move the exponential convergence boundary.

concepts.memory: Multiplication by $t$ in time becomes a negative frequency derivative. Multiplication by an exponential shifts the frequency variable.

sections.title: Solving ordinary differential equations with Laplace transforms

concepts.title: Laplace solutions of ODEs: why the method works
concepts.explain: Transform the differential equation and initial values together into an algebraic equation. Solve for the transformed function, then invert using partial fractions, shifts, or convolution.
concepts.conditions: Take the initial values at $0^+$. Encode piecewise forcing with step functions.
concepts.proof:
Name the unknown transform $Y=\mathcal L[y]$ and the forcing transform $F=\mathcal L[f]$. Write $\mathcal L[y^{\prime}]=pY-y(0)$ and $\mathcal L[y^{\prime\prime}]=p^2Y-py(0)-y^{\prime}(0)$ separately.

After substitution in $y^{\prime\prime}+ay^{\prime}+by=f$, the left side is $p^2Y-py(0)-y^{\prime}(0)+apY-ay(0)+bY$. Keep terms containing $Y$ on the left and move the others right.

This gives $(p^2+ap+b)Y=F+py(0)+y^{\prime}(0)+ay(0)$. It is algebraic; factor the denominator and use partial fractions, shifts, or convolution to invert.

After inversion, check the equation, initial data, and any piecewise matching conditions. Injectivity and applicability of the transform justify the method; a formal inverse expression alone does not replace these checks.

example.question: Solve $y^{\prime}+y=1,\ y(0)=0$.
example.solution:
Let $Y=\mathcal L[y]$. Since $y(0)=0$, the transformed equation is $pY+Y=1/p$, giving $Y=1/[p(p+1)]$.

Decompose as $Y=1/p-1/(p+1)$. The inverse terms are one and $e^{-t}$, giving $y=1-e^{-t}$.

Check $y(0)=0$ and $y^{\prime}=e^{-t}$, hence $y^{\prime}+y=e^{-t}+1-e^{-t}=1$. Both the equation and initial condition hold.

concepts.memory: Write derivative transforms and initial values first → solve for $Y$ → substitute back to check.

exercises.title: Trigonometric functions with absolute values
exercises.question: Expand these periodic functions in Fourier series: (1) $f(x)=|\cos\pi x|$; (2) $f(x)=\sin(\pi x/l)+|\sin(\pi x/l)|$, $l>0$.
exercises.idea: An absolute value can change the period. Use evenness to expand the absolute-value part, then add the known sine term back.
exercises.hint: For (1), use period $1$. For (2), put $\theta=\pi x/l$ and treat $\sin\theta$ and $|\sin\theta|$ separately.
exercises.solution:
(1) The function is even and has period $1$. We have $a_0=2\int_{-1/2}^{1/2}\cos\pi x\,dx=4/\pi$. Product-to-sum identities give
$$a_n=4\int_0^{1/2}\cos\pi x\cos2n\pi x\,dx=\frac{4(-1)^{n+1}}{\pi(4n^2-1)},\quad b_n=0.$$
Hence
$$|\cos\pi x|=\frac2\pi+\frac4\pi\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{(-1)^{n+1}\cos2n\pi x}{4n^2-1}.$$
(2) For $|\sin\theta|$, evenness gives $b_n=0$ and only even-index cosine terms remain: $a_0=4/\pi$, $a_{2n}=-4/[\pi(4n^2-1)]$. The original function also contains $\sin\theta$, so
$$f(x)=\frac2\pi+\sin\frac{\pi x}{l}-\frac4\pi\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{\cos(2n\pi x/l)}{4n^2-1}.$$
Both functions are continuous everywhere, and their series converge to their function values.
exercises.pattern: Remove the absolute value piecewise → find the fundamental period and parity → use product-to-sum → combine known frequencies.
exercises.pitfall: The complete function in (2) is not even. Not all $b_n$ vanish; its coefficient is $b_1=1$.
exercises.verification: Independently derived by integration. The teacher-shared Bilibili image incorrectly omits the sine coefficient in (2); this solution retains $b_1=1$.
exercises.errata: The second function has a nonzero odd part, with sine coefficient $b_1=1$. The public reference image labels every $b_n$ as zero and omits this term.

exercises.title: Identities and a Poisson-kernel expansion
exercises.question: Expand these periodic functions in Fourier series: (1) $f(x)=\cos^2x$; (2) $f(x)=1/[1+\tfrac12\sin x]$.
exercises.idea: Reduce powers in (1). In (2), use a phase shift to put the denominator into the form $1+\frac12\cos t$, then match the Poisson kernel.
exercises.hint: Set $q=2-\sqrt3$ and $r=-q$, and use $1+2\sum_{n\ge1}r^n\cos nt=(1-r^2)/(1-2r\cos t+r^2)$.
exercises.solution:
(1) Power reduction immediately gives $\cos^2x=(1+\cos2x)/2$.
(2) Put $t=x-\pi/2$, giving $\sin x=\cos t$. Choose $r=\sqrt3-2$, which satisfies $-2r/(1+r^2)=1/2$ and $|r|<1$. Add a geometric series and its conjugate:
$$1+2\sum_{n=1}^\infty r^n\cos nt=\frac{1-r^2}{1-2r\cos t+r^2}.$$
Since $(1+r^2)/(1-r^2)=2/\sqrt3$,
$$\frac1{1+\frac12\sin x}=\frac2{\sqrt3}\left[1+2\sum_{n=1}^\infty(\sqrt3-2)^n\cos n\left(x-\frac\pi2\right)\right].$$
This is a valid Fourier series in phase form. For the standard sine-cosine form, split it using $\cos n(x-\pi/2)=\cos nx\cos(n\pi/2)+\sin nx\sin(n\pi/2)$.
exercises.pattern: Try identities first for low-degree trigonometric expressions. For rational trigonometric expressions, try a phase shift and a geometric-series kernel.
exercises.pitfall: Choose the root with modulus less than $1$. The other root cannot give a convergent geometric series.
exercises.verification: Independently derived from the textbook question. Coefficients, boundaries, and transform conventions were checked as applicable.

exercises.title: A periodic sawtooth wave
exercises.question: $f$ has period $2l$ and equals $f(x)=x$ on $[0,2l)$. Find its Fourier series.
exercises.idea: Integrate over any complete period. Relative to the center of this period, the function has a nonzero constant average.
exercises.hint: Use $a_0=2l$. The boundary term in the integration by parts for the sine coefficient does not vanish.
exercises.solution:
Choose one period $[0,2l]$:
$$a_0=\frac1l\int_0^{2l}x\,dx=2l,\qquad a_n=\frac1l\int_0^{2l}x\cos\frac{n\pi x}{l}dx=0.$$
Integration by parts gives
$$b_n=\frac1l\left[-\frac{lx}{n\pi}\cos\frac{n\pi x}{l}+\frac{l^2}{n^2\pi^2}\sin\frac{n\pi x}{l}\right]_0^{2l}=-\frac{2l}{n\pi}.$$
Thus, for $0<x<2l$,
$$x=l-\frac{2l}\pi\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac1n\sin\frac{n\pi x}{l}.$$
At the jumps $x=2kl$, the series sum is $(0+2l)/2=l$. A periodic function cannot take different endpoint values at both ends of a closed period interval. We therefore interpret the textbook interval as half-open.
exercises.answer: $f(x)\sim l-\frac{2l}\pi\sum_{n\ge1}\sin(n\pi x/l)/n$; the sum at a jump is $l$.
exercises.pattern: Integrate over a full period → calculate the average → integrate by parts → state the sum at jumps.
exercises.pitfall: Do not use the oddness of $f=x$ on $[-l,l]$. That defines a different sawtooth.
exercises.verification: Independently integrated and checked against $b_n=-2l/(n\pi)$. The teacher-shared $-l/(n\pi)$ is missing a factor $2$.
exercises.errata: With this site's Fourier-series convention $a_0/2$, the coefficients are $a_0=2l$ and $b_n=-2l/(n\pi)$. The public reference image misses a factor two in the sine coefficient. First align conventions for the constant term.

exercises.title: Sine expansion for zero-value conditions at both ends
exercises.question: On $(0,l)$, let $f(x)=x$. The stated endpoint conditions are $f(0)=f(l)=0$. Find the corresponding Fourier series.
exercises.idea: Interpret the endpoint conditions as selecting sine basis functions that vanish at both ends. In the interior, the function remains $x$.
exercises.hint: Use $\sin(n\pi x/l)$, with coefficients $2l^{-1}\int_0^l x\sin(n\pi x/l)dx$.
exercises.solution:
The sine basis vanishes at both ends. Its projection coefficient is
$$b_n=\frac2l\int_0^l x\sin\frac{n\pi x}{l}dx=\frac{2l(-1)^{n+1}}{n\pi}.$$
Therefore
$$x=\frac{2l}\pi\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{(-1)^{n+1}}n\sin\frac{n\pi x}{l},\quad0<x<l.$$
At endpoints $0,l$, every term and the series sum are zero. The interior function has left-hand endpoint limit $f(l^-)=l$, so the statement “$f=x$ and continuous zero values at both ends” cannot hold simultaneously. There is no contradiction when this is interpreted as an odd-extension or square-integrable expansion of the interior function. Values at isolated endpoints do not change the coefficients.
exercises.answer: $x=\frac{2l}\pi\sum_{n\ge1}(-1)^{n+1}\sin(n\pi x/l)/n$ for $0<x<l$; the endpoint series sum is $0$.
exercises.pattern: Homogeneous value conditions → sine basis → orthogonal projection → discuss endpoints separately.
exercises.pitfall: Do not say that at $x=l$ the expansion converges to $l$. The odd extension has jump average zero there.
exercises.verification: Independently derived from the textbook question. Coefficients, boundaries, and transform conventions were checked as applicable.
exercises.errata: The endpoint conditions choose the extension and eigenfunction basis. When x is incompatible with the prescribed endpoint values, the series recovers the original function in the open interval or in the L² sense.

exercises.title: Cosine expansion for zero-derivative conditions at both ends
exercises.question: On $(0,l)$, let $f(x)=x$, with the stated conditions $f^{\prime}(0)=f^{\prime}(l)=0$. Find the corresponding Fourier series.
exercises.idea: Zero derivatives at both ends select a cosine basis. The interior derivative is $1$, so interpret these conditions as specifying the basis boundary type.
exercises.solution:
Write the cosine expansion as $f=a_0/2+\sum a_n\cos(n\pi x/l)$. Integration gives
$$a_0=\frac2l\int_0^l x\,dx=l,$$
$$a_n=\frac2l\int_0^l x\cos\frac{n\pi x}{l}dx=\frac{2l[(-1)^n-1]}{n^2\pi^2}.$$
The even-index frequency coefficients vanish, so
$$x=\frac l2-\frac{4l}{\pi^2}\sum_{m=0}^\infty\frac{\cos[(2m+1)\pi x/l]}{(2m+1)^2},\quad0\le x\le l.$$
The series recovers continuous function values at the endpoints. But it cannot be differentiated term by term there to conclude $f^{\prime}=0$. The even extension has corners at the endpoints and its derivative is discontinuous.
exercises.pattern: Homogeneous derivative conditions → cosine basis, including the constant mode → integrate by parts twice.
exercises.pitfall: The constant term is $a_0/2$. A valid function expansion does not guarantee term-by-term differentiation at an endpoint.
exercises.verification: Independently derived from the textbook question. Coefficients, boundaries, and transform conventions were checked as applicable.
exercises.errata: The endpoint derivatives of x are incompatible with the stated homogeneous conditions. Endpoint values of the termwise differentiated series cannot be treated as classical endpoint derivatives of the original function.

exercises.title: A mixed expansion: zero derivative at the left, zero value at the right
exercises.question: On $(0,l)$, let $f(x)=x$, with the stated conditions $f^{\prime}(0)=f(l)=0$. Find the corresponding Fourier series.
exercises.idea: Find eigenfunctions satisfying $X^{\prime}(0)=X(l)=0$. This produces a half-integer cosine basis.
exercises.solution:
The condition $X^{\prime}(0)=0$ selects cosine. The condition $X(l)=0$ requires $\cos k_nl=0$, giving $k_n=(n+1/2)\pi/l$. The squared norm is $\int_0^lX_n^2dx=l/2$. Thus
$$c_n=\frac2l\int_0^l x\cos k_nx\,dx=\frac2l\left[\frac{x\sin k_nx}{k_n}+\frac{\cos k_nx}{k_n^2}\right]_0^l=\frac{2(-1)^n}{k_n}-\frac2{lk_n^2}.$$
and
$$x=\sum_{n=0}^\infty\left[\frac{2(-1)^n}{k_n}-\frac2{lk_n^2}\right]\cos k_nx,\quad0<x<l.$$
At $x=l$, every term is zero. The prescribed endpoint conditions are incompatible with a continuous extension of the interior function $x$. Interpret this as an interior or L² expansion in the mixed-boundary basis.
exercises.pattern: For mixed boundaries, solve the eigenvalue condition before projecting. Do not assume integer frequencies.
exercises.pitfall: The derivative is zero on the left and the value is zero on the right. Use half-integer cosines, not half-integer sines.
exercises.verification: Independently derived from the textbook question. Coefficients, boundaries, and transform conventions were checked as applicable.
exercises.errata: If the initial function and endpoint conditions are incompatible, interpret the expansion on the open interval or in L². Discuss endpoint values and termwise differentiation separately.

exercises.title: Transform of a rectangular pulse
exercises.question: Let $f(x)=1$ for $-a\le x\le a$ and $0$ elsewhere, with $a>0$. Find its Fourier transform.
exercises.idea: The function is zero outside its support, so the integration interval shrinks to that support.
exercises.hint: Calculate $\int_{-a}^a e^{-ikx}dx$ directly. Use a limit at $k=0$.
exercises.solution:
With our convention,
$$F(k)=\int_{-a}^a e^{-ikx}dx=\frac{e^{ika}-e^{-ika}}{ik}=\frac{2\sin ak}{k}\quad(k\ne0).$$
Since $\sin ak/k\to a$, fill in $F(0)=2a$. Evenness also gives $2\int_0^a\cos kx\,dx$.
exercises.pattern: Locate the support → use parity → integrate over the finite interval → fill in removable singularities.
exercises.pitfall: $F(0)$ equals the total area of the original function, not zero.
exercises.verification: Independently derived from the textbook question. Coefficients, boundaries, and transform conventions were checked as applicable.

exercises.title: Duality between sinc and a rectangular spectrum
exercises.question: Find the Fourier transform of $f(x)=\sin(ax)/x$ and compare it with the previous exercise. Assume $a>0$ and take the continuous value $a$ at $x=0$.
exercises.idea: Use the inverse transform of the rectangular-pulse result, or split into Dirichlet integrals.
exercises.hint: In the previous exercise, $\mathbf1_{[-a,a]}$ transforms to $2\sin(ax)/x$. Apply duality.
exercises.solution:
Evenness first removes the imaginary part:
$$F(k)=2\int_0^\infty\frac{\sin ax\cos kx}{x}dx=\int_0^\infty\frac{\sin[(a+k)x]+\sin[(a-k)x]}x dx.$$
Use $\int_0^\infty\sin(bx)/x\,dx=(\pi/2)\operatorname{sgn}b$, which is zero when $b=0$. The results are $F=\pi$ for $|k|<a$, $0$ for $|k|>a$, and $\pi/2$ for $|k|=a$. This is the interchange “rectangle ↔ sinc” from the previous exercise; the factor comes from $1/(2\pi)$ in the inverse transform. The integral is a conditionally convergent generalized Fourier transform.
exercises.pattern: For $\sin ax/x$, use rectangular-spectrum duality, or a product-to-sum identity followed by the Dirichlet integral.
exercises.pitfall: At a spectral jump, use the half-value. Do not claim absolute integrability on the whole line.
exercises.verification: Independently derived from the textbook question. Coefficients, boundaries, and transform conventions were checked as applicable.

exercises.title: A two-sided exponential
exercises.question: Find the Fourier transform of $f(x)=e^{-|x|}$.
exercises.idea: Evenness leaves only a cosine integral.
exercises.hint: View $2\int_0^\infty e^{-x}\cos kx\,dx$ as the real part of a complex-exponential integral.
exercises.solution:
Using evenness,
$$F(k)=2\int_0^\infty e^{-x}\cos kx\,dx=2\operatorname{Re}\int_0^\infty e^{-(1-ik)x}dx=2\operatorname{Re}\frac1{1-ik}=\frac2{1+k^2}.$$
At $k=0$ this gives $2$, agreeing with $\int e^{-|x|}dx=2$. The transform is real and even, as expected for a real even original function.
exercises.pattern: Real even function → twice the half-line cosine integral → take the real part of an exponential integral.
exercises.pitfall: Do not replace $|x|$ by $x$ on the entire line.
exercises.verification: Independently derived from the textbook question. Coefficients, boundaries, and transform conventions were checked as applicable.

exercises.title: Transform of a Gaussian
exercises.question: Find the Fourier transform of $f(x)=e^{-x^2}$.
exercises.idea: Differentiate with respect to frequency and integrate by parts. This gives a solvable first-order equation.
exercises.solution:
Let $F(k)=\int e^{-x^2}e^{-ikx}dx$. Gaussian decay is fast enough to justify differentiation under the integral:
$$F^{\prime}(k)=-i\int xe^{-x^2}e^{-ikx}dx=\frac i2\int (e^{-x^2})\prime e^{-ikx}dx=-\frac k2F(k).$$
The solution is $F=C e^{-k^2/4}$. Since $F(0)=\int e^{-x^2}dx=\sqrt\pi$, we obtain $C=\sqrt\pi$. The Gaussian integral follows by squaring it and changing to polar coordinates, giving $\pi$.
exercises.pattern: Gaussian times a polynomial → differentiate in frequency space. Find the basic Gaussian by a differential equation or completing the square.
exercises.pitfall: Another normalization changes the prefactor. This problem uses the textbook convention $F=\int f e^{-ikx}dx$.
exercises.verification: Independently derived from the textbook question. Coefficients, boundaries, and transform conventions were checked as applicable.

exercises.title: A sine function with finite support
exercises.question: Let $f(x)=\sin x$ for $|x|\le\pi$ and $0$ elsewhere. Find its Fourier transform.
exercises.idea: The function is real and odd, so its transform should be purely imaginary and odd.
exercises.hint: Use $\sin x=(e^{ix}-e^{-ix})/(2i)$ and subtract the two finite-interval exponential integrals.
exercises.solution:
By definition,
$$F(k)=\frac1i\left[\frac{\sin\pi(k-1)}{k-1}-\frac{\sin\pi(k+1)}{k+1}\right]=\frac{2i\sin\pi k}{k^2-1}.$$
The points $k=\pm1$ are removable singularities. Direct integration or limits give $F(1)=-i\pi$ and $F(-1)=i\pi$, while $F(0)=0$. These values agree with the purely imaginary odd symmetry.
exercises.pattern: A trigonometric function on a finite interval → split exponentials or use product-to-sum → separately fill in resonant-frequency values.
exercises.pitfall: Do not treat $k=\pm1$ as genuine divergent poles.
exercises.verification: Independently derived from the textbook question. Coefficients, boundaries, and transform conventions were checked as applicable.

exercises.title: A zero boundary on the half-line and odd extension
exercises.question: On $(0,\infty)$, let $f(x)=\cos x$ for $0<x\le\pi$ and $f(x)=0$ for $x>\pi$, with the stated condition $f(0)=0$. Find the corresponding transformed function.
exercises.idea: A zero-value boundary selects an odd extension. Distinguish the half-line sine transform from the whole-line Fourier transform of that extension.
exercises.hint: First calculate $S(k)=\int_0^\pi\cos x\sin kx\,dx$. The whole-line transform of the odd extension is $-2iS(k)$.
exercises.solution:
Define the odd extension $\tilde f(-x)=-f(x)$. Product-to-sum gives
$$S(k)=\frac12\int_0^\pi[\sin(k+1)x+\sin(k-1)x]dx=\frac{k(1+\cos\pi k)}{k^2-1}.$$
Therefore
$$\mathcal F[\tilde f](k)=-2iS(k)=-\frac{2ik(1+\cos\pi k)}{k^2-1}.$$
The continuous values at $k=0,\pm1$ are both zero. If the course uses the sine-transform normalization $\sqrt{2/\pi}$, multiply $S$ by that factor.
The stated $f(0)=0$ is discontinuous with $f(0^+)=1$, but changing a single point does not change the integral. The odd extension has a jump at zero; its series or inverse transform takes the average, zero, there. Since the question does not specify a half-line convention, this solution lists both corresponding transforms explicitly.
exercises.answer: Unnormalized sine transform $S(k)=k(1+\cos\pi k)/(k^2-1)$; whole-line transform of the odd extension $F(k)=-2ik(1+\cos\pi k)/(k^2-1)$, with value zero at removable points.
exercises.pattern: Half-line value boundary → odd extension → sine integral → insert $-2i$ or the normalization factor required by the convention.
exercises.pitfall: With the negative-exponential forward transform the factor is $-2iS$, not $+2iS$.
exercises.verification: Independently checked by product-to-sum. The sign in the teacher-shared whole-line transform conflicts with the textbook's negative-exponential convention and is corrected here.
exercises.errata: The half-line question does not fully specify its transform convention. The solution gives both the sine transform and the whole-line transform of the odd extension. Under $e^{-ikx}$, the latter is a negative purely imaginary odd function; the public reference image has the opposite sign.

exercises.title: The three-dimensional Yukawa potential
exercises.question: Find the three-dimensional Fourier transform of the Yukawa potential $U(r)=e^{-\alpha r}/r$, assuming $\alpha>0$ and $r=|\mathbf r|$. Hint: use spherical coordinates.
exercises.idea: Use the frequency vector as the polar axis. Finish the angular integral before the radial exponential integral.
exercises.solution:
Write $k=|\mathbf k|$. Use the three-dimensional forward transform $\widehat U(\mathbf k)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}U(r)e^{-i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf r}d^3r$. The angular integral is
$$2\pi\int_{-1}^1e^{-ikr\mu}d\mu=4\pi\frac{\sin kr}{kr}.$$
Therefore
$$\widehat U(k)=\frac{4\pi}k\int_0^\infty e^{-\alpha r}\sin kr\,dr=\frac{4\pi}k\frac{k}{\alpha^2+k^2}=\frac{4\pi}{\alpha^2+k^2}.$$
At $k=0$, the continuous value is $4\pi/\alpha^2$, equal to the integral over all space.
exercises.pattern: A radial function in three dimensions → choose $\mathbf k$ as polar axis → reduce the angular integral to sinc → evaluate the one-dimensional radial integral.
exercises.pitfall: The volume element is $r^2\sin\theta\,drd\theta d\phi$. A one-dimensional cosine transform is not a substitute.
exercises.verification: Independently calculated in spherical coordinates. The sign is positive; the negative sign in the teacher-shared image is incorrect. The integral at $k=0$ also checks the positive sign directly.
exercises.errata: Under the convention $\widehat f=\int f e^{-i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf r}d^3r$, the Yukawa-potential transform is positive $4\pi/(k^2+\alpha^2)$. The public reference image has an incorrect overall minus sign.

exercises.title: An inverse-square radial function in three dimensions
exercises.question: Find the three-dimensional Fourier transform of $f(r)=1/r^2$.
exercises.idea: Use the three-dimensional radial formula. The remaining integral is a Dirichlet integral, with regularization needed at infinity.
exercises.solution:
Insert $e^{-\varepsilon r}$, with $\varepsilon>0$, to ensure convergence. The three-dimensional angular integral gives
$$\widehat f_\varepsilon(k)=\frac{4\pi}k\int_0^\infty e^{-\varepsilon r}\frac{\sin kr}{r}dr.$$
Let $J(k)$ denote the radial integral above. Then $J^{\prime}(k)=\int_0^\infty e^{-\varepsilon r}\cos kr\,dr=\varepsilon/(\varepsilon^2+k^2)$ and $J(0)=0$, hence $J=\arctan(k/\varepsilon)$. For $k>0$, let $\varepsilon\to0^+$ to obtain
$$\widehat f(k)=\frac{4\pi}k\frac\pi2=\frac{2\pi^2}k.$$
Thus the generalized Fourier transform is $2\pi^2/|\mathbf k|$. The original function is not integrable over all space, and the spectrum is singular at $k=0$.
exercises.answer: $\widehat f(\mathbf k)=2\pi^2/|\mathbf k|$, interpreted as a distribution.
exercises.pattern: A slowly decaying radial function → insert exponential damping → calculate → take the Abel limit.
exercises.pitfall: The frequency magnitude is $k\ge0$. Do not write $1/k_x$, which would change sign with direction.
exercises.verification: Independently derived by regularization. The minus sign in the teacher-shared image is corrected.
exercises.errata: Regularization or distributions are required. With the same Fourier convention, the result is positive $2\pi^2/|k|$; the public reference image has an incorrect overall sign.

exercises.title: The three-dimensional Coulomb spectrum
exercises.question: Find the Fourier transform of the Coulomb potential $U(r)=1/r$ and compare with the previous exercise. Hint: take the $\alpha=0$ limit of the Yukawa potential.
exercises.idea: Take $\alpha\to0^+$ in the convergent Yukawa transform instead of using a divergent radial integral directly.
exercises.solution:
First take $U_\alpha(r)=e^{-\alpha r}/r$. Exercise 7 gives $\widehat U_\alpha=4\pi/(k^2+\alpha^2)$. As $\alpha\to0^+$, the distributional limit is
$$\widehat{1/r}(\mathbf k)=\frac{4\pi}{|\mathbf k|^2}.$$
In three dimensions, $k^{-2}$ is locally integrable at the origin because the volume element contains $k^2dk$. It is not a continuous spectrum with a finite point value at $k=0$. Compare the previous result $r^{-2}\leftrightarrow2\pi^2/k$: in three dimensions, scaling $r^{-s}$ corresponds to $k^{s-3}$, and $s=1,2$ gives exactly $k^{-2},k^{-1}$.
exercises.answer: $\widehat{1/r}=4\pi/|\mathbf k|^2$ as a distribution; the previous result is $\widehat{1/r^2}=2\pi^2/|\mathbf k|$.
exercises.pattern: A non-absolutely-integrable Coulomb kernel → Yukawa regularization → let the parameter tend to zero → check the scaling power.
exercises.pitfall: $\int_0^\infty\sin kr\,dr$ cannot be evaluated as an ordinary convergent improper integral. State the regularization.
exercises.verification: Independently checked by the Yukawa limit and scaling. The teacher-shared minus sign is corrected.
exercises.errata: The Coulomb potential requires a generalized transform. The result is positive $4\pi/k^2$; the public reference image has an incorrect overall sign. $k=0$ is not an ordinary finite function value.

exercises.title: A squared-sinc integral using Parseval
exercises.question: Use Parseval's theorem to evaluate $I=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\sin^2x/x^2\,dx$.
exercises.idea: Find a rectangular function whose Fourier transform is sinc.
exercises.solution:
With our convention, Parseval's theorem is
$$\int|f(x)|^2dx=\frac1{2\pi}\int|F(k)|^2dk.$$
Choose $f=1$ for $|x|\le1$ and zero elsewhere. The left side is $2$ and the right side is $\frac1{2\pi}\int4\sin^2k/k^2\,dk=2I/\pi$. Therefore $2=2I/\pi$, giving $I=\pi$. At $x=0$, take the continuous value $1$; this does not change the integral.
exercises.pattern: An integral of a square → find a simple function with this spectrum → use Parseval → check normalization.
exercises.pitfall: The inverse-transform factor $1/(2\pi)$ enters Parseval. Omitting it gives the wrong constant.
exercises.verification: Independently derived from the textbook question. Coefficients, boundaries, and transform conventions were checked as applicable.

exercises.title: Rectangular pulses approaching delta
exercises.question: Let $f_h(x)=1/h$ for $|x|\le h/2$ and $0$ elsewhere. Prove that as $h\to0^+$, $f_h\to\delta$.
exercises.idea: Prove convergence of integrals against every test function to its sampled value. Pointwise convergence is not the required statement.
exercises.hint: Set $x=hu$ to turn the integral into $\int_{-1/2}^{1/2}\varphi(hu)du$.
exercises.solution:
For any continuous compactly supported test function $\varphi$,
$$\int_{\mathbb R}f_h(x)\varphi(x)dx=\frac1h\int_{-h/2}^{h/2}\varphi(x)dx=\int_{-1/2}^{1/2}\varphi(hu)du.$$
Since $\varphi$ is continuous at zero, $\varphi(hu)\to\varphi(0)$ holds uniformly on this finite interval. Thus the limit is $\varphi(0)\int_{-1/2}^{1/2}du=\varphi(0)$, exactly the definition of $\delta$. Also $f_h\ge0$, the area is always $1$, and the support shrinks to zero.
exercises.pattern: An approximate-identity proof → check unit area → change variables against a test function → use continuity for the limit.
exercises.pitfall: Their pointwise limit is not an integrable function. “Infinitely high only at zero” is not a sufficient proof.
exercises.verification: Independently derived from the textbook question. Coefficients, boundaries, and transform conventions were checked as applicable.

exercises.title: A two-dimensional delta integral
exercises.question: Evaluate $\int_0^1\int_0^1\delta(x+y-1)dxdy$.
exercises.idea: Fix $y$. The root in $x$ is $1-y$, with derivative $1$.
exercises.hint: For almost every $y\in(0,1)$, the inner integral equals $1$.
exercises.solution:
For $0<y<1$, the root $x=1-y$ lies strictly inside the integration interval, and $\partial(x+y-1)/\partial x=1$. Hence
$$\int_0^1\delta(x+y-1)dx=1.$$
Then integrate over $y$ to get $1$. At $y=0,1$, the roots are on the boundary. Any half-value endpoint convention has no effect on the outer integral because these are just two measure-zero points.
Alternatively, the coarea formula gives a line segment of length $\sqrt2$ inside the square and gradient magnitude $|\nabla(x+y-1)|=\sqrt2$. Their ratio is again $1$.
exercises.pattern: A multidimensional delta → fix the other variables and find a one-variable root → divide by the absolute derivative → finish the remaining integral.
exercises.pitfall: The line length $\sqrt2$ alone is insufficient; divide by the gradient magnitude too.
exercises.verification: Independently derived from the textbook question. Coefficients, boundaries, and transform conventions were checked as applicable.

exercises.title: Generalized transform of the sign function
exercises.question: Let $\operatorname{sgn}x=1$ for $x>0$ and $-1$ for $x<0$. Find its Fourier transform.
exercises.idea: The ordinary integral does not converge. Use a damping limit or a distributional derivative.
exercises.hint: Since $\operatorname{sgn}\prime=2\delta$, we have $ikF=2$. Oddness excludes an additional $\delta(k)$ term.
exercises.solution:
Insert even damping $e^{-\varepsilon|x|}$:
$$F_\varepsilon(k)=\int_0^\infty e^{-\varepsilon x}e^{-ikx}dx-\int_0^\infty e^{-\varepsilon x}e^{ikx}dx=\frac{-2ik}{\varepsilon^2+k^2}.$$
As $\varepsilon\to0^+$, the distributional limit is $k/(k^2+\varepsilon^2)\to\operatorname{PV}(1/k)$, so
$$\mathcal F[\operatorname{sgn}x]=-2i\operatorname{PV}\frac1k=\frac2i\operatorname{PV}\frac1k.$$
Check by multiplying by $ik$ to get $2$, in agreement with $\mathcal F[2\delta]=2$. The result is a purely imaginary odd distribution, so it has no even $\delta(k)$ contribution.
exercises.pattern: A nondecaying function → exponential regularization or distributional differentiation → use parity to determine possible delta terms.
exercises.pitfall: $1/k$ must be labeled as a principal value. The ordinary improper Fourier integral does not exist.
exercises.verification: Independently derived from the textbook question. Coefficients, boundaries, and transform conventions were checked as applicable.

exercises.title: Fourier transform of a product
exercises.question: Given $\mathcal F[f]=F$ and $\mathcal F[g]=G$, prove $\mathcal F[fg]=(F*G)/(2\pi)$, where $(F*G)(k)=\int F(k_1)G(k-k_1)dk_1$.
exercises.idea: Write one factor as an inverse transform, then interchange the integrations.
exercises.solution:
First prove the formula for Schwartz functions, which are smooth and rapidly decaying, so the interchange is justified:
$$\mathcal F[fg](k)=\int g(x)e^{-ikx}\left[\frac1{2\pi}\int F(q)e^{iqx}dq\right]dx$$
$$=\frac1{2\pi}\int F(q)\left[\int g(x)e^{-i(k-q)x}dx\right]dq=\frac1{2\pi}\int F(q)G(k-q)dq.$$
This is the required result. It extends to other integrable cases when the interchange and inverse-transform conditions hold. Products of general distributions need a separate definition and cannot use this formula unconditionally.
exercises.pattern: To transform a product → expand one inverse transform → interchange using Fubini → recognize the other transform.
exercises.pitfall: With this convention, a time-domain convolution transforms to a product. A time-domain product introduces an extra $1/(2\pi)$ in its transformed convolution.
exercises.verification: Independently derived from the textbook question. Coefficients, boundaries, and transform conventions were checked as applicable.

exercises.title: Generalized spectrum of a causal sine
exercises.question: Find the Fourier transform of $f(x)=h(x)\sin(\omega x)$, where $h$ is the unit step function.
exercises.idea: First damp $h$, or use $\mathcal F[h]=\pi\delta+\operatorname{PV}(1/(ik))$ together with frequency shifts.
exercises.hint: Split sine into two exponentials. Their spectra shift to $k=\pm\omega$.
exercises.solution:
For $\varepsilon>0$,
$$F_\varepsilon(k)=\int_0^\infty e^{-(\varepsilon+ik)x}\sin\omega x\,dx=\frac1{2i}\left[\frac1{\varepsilon+i(k-\omega)}-\frac1{\varepsilon+i(k+\omega)}\right].$$
Use $\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}(\varepsilon+is)^{-1}=\pi\delta(s)+(1/i)\operatorname{PV}(1/s)$ to obtain
$$F(k)=\frac\pi{2i}[\delta(k-\omega)-\delta(k+\omega)]-\frac12\left[\operatorname{PV}\frac1{k-\omega}-\operatorname{PV}\frac1{k+\omega}\right].$$
Equivalently, the nondelta part is $\omega\operatorname{PV}[1/(\omega^2-k^2)]$, with a separate principal value at each pole. At $\omega=0$, both parts cancel to zero.
exercises.pattern: A step-truncated harmonic → damp it for convergence → apply frequency shifts → retain both principal-value and delta terms.
exercises.pitfall: Giving only $\omega/(\omega^2-k^2)$ omits the delta contributions at resonant frequencies.
exercises.verification: Independently derived from the textbook question. Coefficients, boundaries, and transform conventions were checked as applicable.

exercises.title: Laplace transform of sine
exercises.question: Find the Laplace transform of $\sin(at)$.
exercises.idea: Write sine as complex exponentials.
exercises.solution:
For $\operatorname{Re}p>0$, with $a$ real,
$$\mathcal L[\sin at]=\frac1{2i}\left(\frac1{p-ia}-\frac1{p+ia}\right)=\frac a{p^2+a^2}.$$
At $a=0$, both the original function and its transform are zero.
exercises.pattern: A trigonometric function → split into exponentials → combine two simple fractions.
exercises.pitfall: The numerator is $a$, not $p$; the latter belongs to cosine.
exercises.verification: Independently derived from the textbook question. Coefficients, boundaries, and transform conventions were checked as applicable.

exercises.title: Hyperbolic sine and cosine
exercises.question: Find the Laplace transforms of $\sinh(at)$ and $\cosh(at)$.
exercises.idea: Hyperbolic functions are already sums or differences of real exponentials.
exercises.hint: Use $(e^{at}\mp e^{-at})/2$ for the two cases.
exercises.solution:
When $\operatorname{Re}p>|a|$,
$$\mathcal L[\sinh at]=\frac12\left(\frac1{p-a}-\frac1{p+a}\right)=\frac a{p^2-a^2},$$
$$\mathcal L[\cosh at]=\frac12\left(\frac1{p-a}+\frac1{p+a}\right)=\frac p{p^2-a^2}.$$
The convergence half-plane requires both exponential terms to decay.
exercises.pattern: Split into real exponentials → transform each → check the largest growth rate.
exercises.pitfall: Hyperbolic-function denominators have a minus sign. Ordinary trigonometric-function denominators have a plus sign.
exercises.verification: Independently derived from the textbook question. Coefficients, boundaries, and transform conventions were checked as applicable.

exercises.title: The time-multiplication property
exercises.question: Find the Laplace transform of $t\cos(at)$.
exercises.idea: Multiplying by $t$ in time corresponds to a negative derivative of the transformed function.
exercises.solution:
Differentiate the defining integral with respect to $p$: $F^{\prime}(p)=-\int_0^\infty t f(t)e^{-pt}dt$. Therefore
$$\mathcal L[t\cos at]=-\frac d{dp}\frac p{p^2+a^2}=\frac{p^2-a^2}{(p^2+a^2)^2},\quad\operatorname{Re}p>0.$$
At $a=0$, the result is $1/p^2$, agreeing with $\mathcal L[t]$.
exercises.pattern: For the transform of $t^nf(t)$ → apply $(-1)^n$ times the $n$th derivative to the transformed function.
exercises.pitfall: Differentiate first, then take the negative. The quotient rule can easily introduce a lost minus sign.
exercises.verification: Independently derived from the textbook question. Coefficients, boundaries, and transform conventions were checked as applicable.

exercises.title: Exponential shift
exercises.question: Find the Laplace transforms of $e^{bt}\sin(at)$ and $e^{bt}\cosh(at)$.
exercises.idea: Multiplication by $e^{bt}$ replaces $p$ by $p-b$ in the defining transform.
exercises.hint: Apply $p\mapsto p-b$ to the corresponding basic transforms.
exercises.solution:
Using $e^{bt}e^{-pt}=e^{-(p-b)t}$,
$$\mathcal L[e^{bt}\sin at]=\frac a{(p-b)^2+a^2},\quad\operatorname{Re}p>b,$$
$$\mathcal L[e^{bt}\cosh at]=\frac{p-b}{(p-b)^2-a^2},\quad\operatorname{Re}p>b+|a|.$$
Shift the numerator of the second formula as well.
exercises.pattern: Multiplication by an exponential → shift the entire transformed function → shift the convergence region too.
exercises.pitfall: The numerator in the second formula is the first power $p-b$, not $(p-b)^2$.
exercises.verification: Independently checked from the definition. The squared numerator in the teacher-shared hyperbolic-cosine transform is a typo and is corrected here.
exercises.errata: The numerator of $\mathcal L[e^{bt}\cosh at]$ is $p-b$. The public reference image gives $(p-b)^2$, which disagrees with both direct integration and a dimensional check.

exercises.title: Inverse Laplace transforms
exercises.question: Find the original functions: (1) $(p-2)/[(p-2)^2+4]$; (2) $-1/[p^2(p-1)]$.
exercises.idea: In (1), recognize cosine and an exponential shift. In (2), use partial fractions.
exercises.solution:
(1) Compare with $\mathcal L[\cos2t]=p/(p^2+4)$ and replace $p$ by $p-2$. The original function is $e^{2t}\cos2t$.
(2) Set $-1/[p^2(p-1)]=A/p+B/p^2+C/(p-1)$. Multiplying by the denominator gives $-1=Ap(p-1)+B(p-1)+Cp^2$. Setting $p=0,1$ gives $B=1,C=-1$. Matching the linear coefficient gives $A=1$. Thus the inverse transform is $1+t-e^t$.
exercises.pattern: Recognize a standard transform first. If that fails, decompose into simple or repeated poles.
exercises.pitfall: $1/p^2$ corresponds to $t$. Carry the minus sign through the entire partial-fraction calculation.
exercises.verification: Independently derived from the textbook question. Coefficients, boundaries, and transform conventions were checked as applicable.

exercises.title: The Laplace integration theorem
exercises.question: Prove $\mathcal L[\int_0^t f(\tau)d\tau]=F(p)/p$.
exercises.idea: Reverse the integration order over the triangular domain.
exercises.solution:
For sufficiently large $\operatorname{Re}p$ and absolute convergence,
$$\mathcal L\left[\int_0^t f(\tau)d\tau\right]=\int_0^\infty\int_0^t f(\tau)e^{-pt}d\tau dt$$
$$=\int_0^\infty f(\tau)\left[\int_\tau^\infty e^{-pt}dt\right]d\tau=\frac1p\int_0^\infty f(\tau)e^{-p\tau}d\tau=\frac{F(p)}p.$$
Alternatively, set $g=\int_0^tf$. Then $g^{\prime}=f,g(0)=0$, and the derivative theorem gives $pG=F$.
exercises.pattern: For a time-integral theorem → interchange integrals in the definition, or use a derivative relation with zero initial value.
exercises.pitfall: The lower limit is zero. An extra integration constant would transform to that constant divided by $p$.
exercises.verification: Independently derived from the textbook question. Coefficients, boundaries, and transform conventions were checked as applicable.

exercises.title: A second-order nonhomogeneous initial-value problem
exercises.question: Solve $y^{\prime\prime}+2y^{\prime}-3y=e^{-t}$ for $t>0$, with $y(0)=0,y^{\prime}(0)=1$.
exercises.idea: Insert the initial values into the derivative transforms first. The initial velocity contributes to the transformed right-hand side.
exercises.solution:
Transforming gives
$$(p^2Y-1)+2pY-3Y=\frac1{p+1},\qquad Y=\frac{p+2}{(p+1)(p-1)(p+3)}.$$
The partial fractions are
$$Y=\frac{3/8}{p-1}-\frac{1/4}{p+1}-\frac{1/8}{p+3}.$$
Invert term by term to obtain $y=\frac38e^t-\frac14e^{-t}-\frac18e^{-3t}$. Check $y(0)=0$ and $y^{\prime}(0)=3/8+1/4+3/8=1$. Under the operator $D^2+2D-3$, both homogeneous exponentials vanish and $-e^{-t}/4$ produces $e^{-t}$.
exercises.pattern: Include initial-value corrections → solve the rational transformed equation → use partial fractions → invert → check both initial values and the equation.
exercises.pitfall: $\mathcal L[y^{\prime\prime}]=p^2Y-1$. Do not omit the initial velocity.
exercises.verification: Independently derived from the textbook question. Coefficients, boundaries, and transform conventions were checked as applicable.

exercises.title: An oscillator with constant forcing
exercises.question: Solve $y^{\prime\prime}+y=2$ for $t>0$, with $y(0)=0,y^{\prime}(0)=1$.
exercises.idea: The transform of a constant is $2/p$. Separate sine and $1-\cos t$ terms.
exercises.solution:
The transformed equation is $(p^2+1)Y-1=2/p$. Therefore
$$Y=\frac1{p^2+1}+\frac2{p(p^2+1)}=\frac1{p^2+1}+\frac2p-\frac{2p}{p^2+1}.$$
Inversion gives $y=\sin t+2-2\cos t$. We have $y(0)=0,y^{\prime}(0)=1$ and $y^{\prime\prime}+y=2$.
exercises.pattern: Constant forcing → $1/p$ → recognize $1/[p(p^2+\omega^2)]$.
exercises.pitfall: The transform of the constant $2$ is $2/p$, not $2$.
exercises.verification: Independently derived from the textbook question. Coefficients, boundaries, and transform conventions were checked as applicable.

exercises.title: Three parameter regimes of an oscillator
exercises.question: Use Laplace transforms to solve $y^{\prime\prime}+\lambda y=0$ for $t>0$, with $y(0)=a,y^{\prime}(0)=b$.
exercises.idea: Positive, zero, and negative $\lambda$ give oscillation, uniform motion, and hyperbolic growth, respectively.
exercises.solution:
The derivative transform gives $(p^2+\lambda)Y=ap+b$.
1. If $\lambda=\omega^2>0$, then $Y=ap/(p^2+\omega^2)+b/(p^2+\omega^2)$, so $y=a\cos\omega t+(b/\omega)\sin\omega t$.
2. If $\lambda=0$, then $Y=a/p+b/p^2$, so $y=a+bt$.
3. If $\lambda=-\mu^2<0$, then $Y=ap/(p^2-\mu^2)+b/(p^2-\mu^2)$, so $y=a\cosh\mu t+(b/\mu)\sinh\mu t$.
Each formula satisfies the initial values in its parameter range. The limit as $\lambda\to0$ also gives $a+bt$.
exercises.pattern: A parameter-dependent second-order equation → obtain one transformed formula → classify the inverse by denominator-root type.
exercises.pitfall: If the question does not assume $\lambda>0$, include the zero and negative cases.
exercises.verification: Independently derived from the textbook question. Coefficients, boundaries, and transform conventions were checked as applicable.

exercises.title: A force acting for a finite time
exercises.question: Solve $y^{\prime\prime}+4y=f(t)$ with $y(0)=1,y^{\prime}(0)=0$, where $f(t)=1$ for $0<t<t_0$ and $0$ for $t>t_0$, with $t_0>0$.
exercises.idea: The force switches on and later switches off. Represent it as the difference of two steps.
exercises.solution:
The force transforms to $F=(1-e^{-pt_0})/p$. Thus
$$Y=\frac p{p^2+4}+\frac{1-e^{-pt_0}}{p(p^2+4)}.$$
Since $\mathcal L^{-1}[1/(p(p^2+4))]=(1-\cos2t)/4$, the delay theorem gives
$$y(t)=\cos2t+\frac{1-\cos2t}4-\frac{H(t-t_0)}4[1-\cos2(t-t_0)].$$
Equivalently, for $0\le t\le t_0$ use $y=1/4+(3/4)\cos2t$, and for $t>t_0$ use $y=(3/4)\cos2t+(1/4)\cos2(t-t_0)$. Both $y,y^{\prime}$ are continuous at $t_0$. The step in the force only makes $y^{\prime\prime}$ jump.
exercises.pattern: Piecewise force → difference of steps → solve in transform space → subtract the delayed response → check joining conditions.
exercises.pitfall: In a delayed term, replace $t$ by $t-t_0$ and also multiply by $H(t-t_0)$.
exercises.verification: Independently derived from the textbook question. Coefficients, boundaries, and transform conventions were checked as applicable.

exercises.title: A coupled system of differential equations
exercises.question: Solve $y^{\prime\prime}-x^{\prime\prime}+x^{\prime}-y=e^t-2$ and $2y^{\prime\prime}-x^{\prime\prime}-2y^{\prime}+x=-t$ with initial values $x(0)=x^{\prime}(0)=y(0)=y^{\prime}(0)=0$.
exercises.idea: All initial values are zero. The transforms give two linear algebraic equations for the two transformed functions.
exercises.solution:
Write $X=\mathcal L[x],Y=\mathcal L[y]$. Zero initial values give
$$(p^2-1)Y+(-p^2+p)X=\frac1{p-1}-\frac2p,$$
$$(2p^2-2p)Y+(-p^2+1)X=-\frac1{p^2}.$$
Elimination yields
$$X=\frac{2p-1}{p^2(p-1)^2}=\frac1{(p-1)^2}-\frac1{p^2},$$
$$Y=\frac1{p(p-1)^2}=\frac1p-\frac1{p-1}+\frac1{(p-1)^2}.$$
Thus $x=t(e^t-1)$ and $y=1-e^t+te^t$. Differentiation gives $x^{\prime}=e^t(1+t)-1,x^{\prime\prime}=e^t(2+t)$ and $y^{\prime}=te^t,y^{\prime\prime}=(1+t)e^t$. Substitution into the first equation gives $e^t-2$ and into the second gives $-t$. All initial values are zero.
exercises.pattern: A coupled constant-coefficient linear system → transform into algebra → eliminate two unknowns → invert partial fractions → check each original equation.
exercises.pitfall: The second equation contains $-2y^{\prime}$, not $-2y$. Read the derivative order carefully.
exercises.verification: Independently derived algebraically. SymPy partial fractions and direct substitution into each original equation agree.
